The discretion vested in an Appellate Court under Order XLI Rule 27, C.P.C. is not intended to enable a party to fill lacunae in its case or to introduce evidence which, despite having the opportunity, was not produced before the Trial Court.

Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines “gift” as the transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration, by one person, called the donor, to another, called the donee, and accepted by or on behalf of the donee.

Section 123 thereof prescribes the mode of making a gift of immovable property and requires that such gift be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses.

The governing principle is embodied in Section 11 of the Contract Act, 1872, which provides that every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 16 of the Contract Act, 1872 defines undue influence and provides, inter alia, that a contract is induced by undue influence where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of them is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other.

Registration is not a substitute for proof of voluntary execution by a donor possessing the requisite mental capacity, nor can it dispense with the statutory requirements of execution and attestation under Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

So far as the revisional jurisdiction of this Court is concerned, Section 115, C.P.C. does not confer upon the High Court an unrestricted appellate jurisdiction to reassess the entire evidence merely because another view may conceivably be taken.
The impugned judgments and decrees are consequently found to be well founded and do not warrant interference under Section 115, C.P.C.

It was contended that the learned trial Court rightly exercised its discretion under Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. to prevent unnecessary continuation of the proceedings.

In view of the rival submissions, the following question arises for determination: Whether, in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the learned trial Court lawfully invoked Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. to close the appellants' right to adduce evidence, and if not, whether the review petition preferred against the said order was maintainable notwithstanding the availability of an appellate
At the very outset we observe that Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. is a penal provision.

In such circumstances, the indispensable condition for invoking Order XVII Rule 3 CPC, that time had been granted to the defaulting party for performing an act necessary for the progress of the suit, stood conspicuously absent.

In Qutab-ud-Din v. Gulzar (PLD 1991 SC 1109), this Court categorically held that where the previous adjournment was not granted on the request of the plaintiff, Order XVII Rule 3 CPC could not be invoked for closing the plaintiff's evidence.

The above principle finds reaffirmation in Muhammad Aslam v. Nazir Ahmed (2008 SCMR 942) wherein this Court explained that Order XVII Rule 3 does not authorise dismissal of the suit merely because evidence is not produced on a particular date.

As explained by this Court in Rana Tanveer Khan v. Naseer-ud-Din (2015 SCMR 1401), the decisive consideration is not merely the number of adjournments but whether those opportunities had been availed at the request of the party and whether the case had truly fallen within the mischief of Order XVII Rule 3.

The order dated 14.10.2009, whereby the learned trial Court invoked the provisions of Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. and closed the appellants' right to adduce evidence, is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is, accordingly, set aside.

Had the learned trial Court considered that the repeated defaults had reached a stage warranting invocation of the penal provisions of Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C., it could have exercised such jurisdiction on one of those occasions, subject always to the fulfilment of the statutory requirements.

Trial Courts are equally entrusted with maintaining discipline in judicial proceedings and must adhere to the provisions of Order XVII, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which permit the adjournment of a case only where ‘sufficient cause’ is shown.

If the Court genuinely considers that the default warrants the consequences contemplated by law, it should not hesitate to invoke the relevant statutory provision, including Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C., where its conditions are satisfied.
